summary: This document provides a framework for Data Center Network Virtualization over Layer 3 and defines a reference model with the logical components needed to design a solution.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes a framework for virtual tenant networks carried over a data-center IP network. It defines the main components and explains issues such as control, mobility, multicast, path size, and security.

subtitle: A reference architecture for providing tenant networks over a Layer 3 data-center underlay.

tldr.problem: Large data centers need logical networks for tenants that remain separate while sharing an IP network infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines Network Virtualization Edges, tenant network instances, access points, context identifiers, and tunnels over an IP underlay.
tldr.outcome: It provides a reference model and highlights design issues for later solutions. It does not specify one tunneling or control-plane protocol.

today: RFC 7365 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo presents a framework rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Overlay and Its Terms
sections.content:
Network Virtualization over Layer 3 (NVO3) provides Layer 2 or Layer 3 services to tenant systems over an IP underlay. The underlay carries encapsulated tenant packets and does not need to know that it is carrying NVO3 traffic.

A Virtual Network (VN) is a logical network for tenant systems. A Network Virtualization Edge (NVE) sits at the edge of the underlay and performs the virtualization functions. An NVE can be implemented in a hypervisor's virtual switch, in a physical network device, in a network-service appliance, or across multiple devices.
sections.plainLanguage: The overlay is a virtual network for tenant systems, while the underlay is the IP network that carries its packets. An NVE connects tenant-facing systems to that underlay.

sections.title: Reference Model and NVE Services
sections.content:
An NVE provides a logical connection between tenant systems that belong to a virtual network. It may learn reachability directly from other NVEs or obtain it from a Network Virtualization Authority (NVA). NVAs can be clustered for redundancy and scalability.

A Tenant System connects to a Virtual Network Instance (VNI) through a Virtual Access Point (VAP). An NVE can provide an L2 service that resembles an Ethernet LAN, an L3 service that provides per-tenant IP forwarding, or both. The forwarding sub-layer uses the IP underlay to tunnel traffic between NVEs.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVE connects a tenant's system to the right virtual network. It can provide Ethernet-like service, IP-routing service, or both.

sections.title: Tenant Context and Tunneling
sections.content:
Each VNI holds a forwarding context with reachability information and policies. To separate multiple tenant services on one underlay, an NVE includes a Virtual Network Context identifier along with tunnel information. The receiving NVE uses that context to select the correct tenant service.

The framework describes identifiers at the tenant, VNI, or VAP level. Once the context is identified, the NVE tunnels the tenant packet to the destination NVE. The memo lists GRE, L2TP, IPsec, and MPLS as possible tunneling options, and describes both stateless and stateful tunneling.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet carries information that identifies its tenant context, so the receiving NVE can deliver it to the correct virtual network. An outer tunnel carries it across the IP underlay.

sections.title: Control, Multihoming, and VM Mobility
sections.content:
Control and management can be centralized, distributed, or combined. NVEs need information that maps tenant systems to VNIs and destination systems to egress NVEs. That information may come from a control protocol, management system, or data-plane learning. The source of tenant-system information must be checked so that it is not spoofed or altered.

Multihoming can improve reliability between tenant systems, access switches, core nodes, and data-center gateways. When an NVE provides an L2 service and is separate from the tenant system, loop-avoidance techniques are needed. The memo also discusses moving virtual machines: hot mobility requires preserving the VM's L2 and L3 addresses and maintaining NVE connectivity policies.
sections.plainLanguage: NVEs need to learn where tenant systems are and which network they belong to. Multiple attachments can help with failures, and a VM move must preserve the connectivity the tenant expects.

sections.title: Overlay Design Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Overlays keep unicast tunnel state at the network edge, hide tenant addresses from the underlay, and separate tenant address spaces. They can also reduce forwarding state in the underlay. However, an overlay may not know underlay utilization, and uncoordinated overlays can use resources inefficiently. Overlay traffic may also encounter firewalls or NAT devices.

For broadcast, unknown unicast, and multicast traffic, the memo compares ingress replication with underlay multicast trees as a bandwidth-versus-state trade-off. Encapsulation adds header size, so the underlay MTU should accommodate the tunnel overhead where possible. NVE placement depends on processing, memory, multicast, QoS, and resiliency needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Overlays separate tenant traffic and reduce the state needed in the underlay. They also add headers and can make it harder to see congestion or coordinate resource use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The service must meet agreed tenant security requirements, and the network must trust the virtual-network identity on packets received from a tenant. VNIs and tunnels separate one tenant's traffic from another's, but the memo says that the overlay encapsulation itself does not receive integrity protection after the tenant is verified.

Control traffic among NVEs and NVAs, access to those systems, and management systems must be secured. If the underlay is not trusted to provide data integrity, the memo says encryption is needed. A tenant may also encrypt its data before sending it into the service.
sections.plainLanguage: Tenant separation helps keep traffic in its proper context, but it does not authenticate every overlay header. Control systems and tenant identity must be protected, and encryption may be needed across an untrusted underlay.
